summary: This document describes two methods for producing an integrity check value from a Diffie-Hellman key pair and one from an elliptic curve key pair. It is needed for tasks like signing a PKCS #10 certification request. The algorithms prove possession of the private key and are not a general-purpose signing algorithm. It obsoletes an earlier RFC.

eli5.summary: This shows how to prove you own a secret key without giving the key away, like showing you can open a lock without handing over the key.

questions: how to prove possession of a dh private key
what is proof of possession in pkix
subtitle: How to prove you hold a Diffie-Hellman private key when the key cannot sign.

tldr.problem: A certification request (PKCS #10) normally proves key possession with a signature, but Diffie-Hellman and ECDH keys are key agreement keys and cannot sign or encrypt directly.
tldr.mechanism: Two methods derive a shared secret with the recipient's certificate key and compute a MAC over the request, and a third is a modified DSA-style signature that works with any verifier.
tldr.outcome: The algorithms prove possession of the private key and are not meant as general purpose signing algorithms. RFC 6955 obsoletes RFC 2875.

facts.label: POP methods
facts.value: 3 (static DH, discrete log signature, static ECDH)

today: RFC 6955 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2013. It obsoletes RFC 2875, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Proof-of-Possession Matters
sections.content:
A Certification Authority (CA) must check who is asking for a certificate, and also that the requester holds the private key matching the public key to be certified. That check is called Proof-of-Possession (POP).

PKCS #10 (RFC 2986) assumes the key can produce a signature. The Certificate Request Message Format (RFC 4211) has another method for encryption-only keys, but PKCS #10 does not. Diffie-Hellman (DH) and Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) are key agreement algorithms and cannot be used directly for signing or encryption.

This document supplies three POP algorithms. Two use key agreement to get a shared secret, one for DH and one for ECDH, and are built for a specific verifier. The third is a modified signature algorithm for DH that allows arbitrary verifiers.
sections.eli5: When you ask for an ID card, the office wants proof the secret code is really yours. This RFC gives ways to prove it for keys that cannot sign their name.

sections.title: Static DH Proof-of-Possession
sections.content:
This method needs a key derivation function (KDF) and a MAC, and both sides must use the same group parameters. The requester picks them from a certificate belonging to the recipient, so a certificate with the right group parameters must be available. The recipient's key pair is Rpub and Rpriv, and the requester generates its own pair with the same parameters.

To compute the POP the requester takes the value to sign (for PKCS #10, the DER-encoded certificationRequestInfo) and computes the shared secret ZZ as g^(x*y) mod p. It derives a temporary key K = KDF(LeadingInfo | ZZ | TrailingInfo), where LeadingInfo is the recipient certificate's Subject Distinguished Name and TrailingInfo is its Issuer Distinguished Name. The result is MAC(K, text).

The recipient repeats the computation and compares. A match shows the requester has the private key, because it was needed for the shared secret, and that only the intended recipient could verify, because that needs the recipient's own private key. When the recipient is a CA, this protects the requester from rogue CAs.
sections.eli5: You and a friend each hold half of a secret handshake. Only someone with their half can do the full handshake, so doing it right proves you have yours.

sections.title: ASN.1 Encoding and Hash Choices
sections.content:
The signature value is a DhSigStatic structure: an optional issuerAndSerial and a hashValue holding the MAC result. The issuer and serial number identify the certificate the public key came from, and are omitted if the key did not come from a certificate. The algorithm parameters MUST be absent.

The RFC defines object identifiers for SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, using HMAC as the MAC. The SHA-1 identifier keeps the same value as the one from RFC 2875, and the SHA-2 variants are new, under id-pkix id-alg(6) with numbers 15 to 18.
sections.eli5: The answer is written on a standard form, and a code on the form says which scrambling recipe was used.

sections.title: The Discrete Logarithm Signature
sections.content:
A single shared parameter set for many keys raises the chance of collisions, and lets an attacker go after the whole set at once. So the RFC also defines a POP for DH keys that needs no common parameters. It is based on DSA, but drops the size limits that FIPS 186-3 sets, so it requires only that q be at least b bits, where b is the hash output size. Keys generated with the method in RFC 2631 meet the extra requirement of having a q parameter.

If q is longer than the hash output, the digest is expanded by repeatedly appending the hash of the value so far and then keeping the leftmost L-1 bits. This adds no security beyond the hash's own b bits, so the hash should be as large as possible to match q.

Signing yields a pair (r, s) with a random k, r = (g^k mod p) mod q and s = (k^-1 * (m + x*r)) mod q, repeating if either is zero. Verification is stricter than plain DSA: the verifier must strongly check that p and q are prime and that q divides p-1 before checking r and s are in range and recomputing v to compare with r.

The signature algorithm is parameterized by hash (SHA-1 through SHA-512, under id-alg(6) numbers 4 to 8). The DomainParameters SHOULD be omitted in the signature but MUST be present in the associated key request.
sections.eli5: This is a way to sign your name that anyone can check, even if you never met them before. Everyone has to check the math carefully so nobody can trick them.

sections.title: Static ECDH Proof-of-Possession
sections.content:
The elliptic curve version follows the same steps as the DH one. The requester takes the group G from the recipient's certificate, which for PKIX is almost always a named group. The requester generates a pair with Epub = Epriv * G and computes the shared secret point as Epriv * Rpub. ZZ is the x coordinate of that point. The key K and the MAC are derived exactly as in the DH case.

The same conclusions hold: the requester has the private key, and only the intended recipient can verify. The ASN.1 reuses DhSigStatic and defines identifiers for SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 with HMAC, numbered 25 to 28 under id-alg(6). The key type is pk-ec.

The RFC did not create an ECDSA-like signature variant. With ECDH the usual practice is a predefined curve paired with a hash, so a key able to do the modified algorithm should be able to use regular ECDSA with the correctly sized hash.
sections.eli5: Same secret handshake, but done with a different kind of math that uses points on a curve.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
None of these algorithms is for general purpose use. They exist only to do POP with PKCS #10 and CRMF.

In the static DH and static ECDH methods either party can produce a valid value, so they give integrity but not origination. The Discrete Logarithm Signature gives both integrity and origination checking.

All security rests on the secrecy of the private keys. If a sender's or recipient's key is disclosed, all messages using it are compromised. Parameter choice matters: it must fit the community of entities and avoid small groups, and the RFC points to FIPS 186-3 and Section 10 of RFC 6090 for guidance.
sections.eli5: The whole thing is only as safe as the secret key. Lose it or share it, and the proof means nothing.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 2875
sections.content: Compared with RFC 2875, the Static DH algorithm was rewritten so the hash and MAC are parameters. New instances use HMAC with SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, while the SHA-1 one stays identical. The Discrete Logarithm Signature was likewise parameterized by hash and gained the same new instances. The Static ECDH algorithm is entirely new.
sections.eli5: The old recipe only used one kind of scrambler. The new one lets you choose stronger ones, and adds a curve version.
